title: Dot products & the prediction equation
intro: The mathematical foundation of the course: one ingredient — the dot product — describes exactly how every linear classifier predicts.
keyPoints: The dot product x·w + b is the raw model output: the score before thresholding.
In NumPy: X @ coef_.T + intercept_ — literally what decision_function() does.
Every linear classifier (LR, SVM) uses exactly the same prediction equation.
The sign of the raw output picks the class: positive → class 1, negative → class 0.

blocks.html: The dot product: multiply two vectors element-wise and add everything up. With x = [0, 1, 2] and y = [3, 4, 5]: 0+4+10 = 14. In Python: x @ y.

blocks.label: dot product
blocks.caption: In numpy: x @ y — element-wise multiplication and summation.
The dot product in numpy
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([0, 1, 2])
y = np.array([3, 4, 5])

print('x * y (element-wise):', x * y)
print('sum of that         :', sum(x * y))
print('x @ y (dot product) :', x @ y)

sections.title: The prediction equation of linear classifiers

blocks.html: Every linear classifier predicts in two steps: (1) the raw model output \( w \cdot x + b \) (learned coef_ and intercept_), (2) only the sign: positive → positive class. The pattern is identical for logistic regression and linear SVMs — the difference lies entirely in the loss used for fitting.

blocks.label: raw model output
blocks.latex: f(x) \;=\; w \cdot x + b \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{p} w_i x_i + b
blocks.caption: w = coefficients (lr.coef_), b = intercept (lr.intercept_).

blocks.label: prediction
blocks.caption: Positive → positive class, negative → negative class (scikit-learn translates this into the class names of your data).
Rebuilding predict() yourself with coef_ and intercept_
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=10000).fit(X, y)

for i in (10, 20):
    raw = lr.coef_ @ X[i] + lr.intercept_
    print(f'example {i:2d}: raw = {raw[0]:+8.3f}  '
          f'sign = {np.sign(raw[0]):+2.0f}  '
          f'lr.predict = {lr.predict([X[i]])[0]}')

blocks.html: See how predict does nothing but translate the sign of the raw model output back into class names (here 0 and 1). Same outcome, for every linear classifier.

sections.title: Seeing the boundary: coefficients and intercept steer it

blocks.html: On the decision boundary the raw output is exactly zero; the sign tells you which side you are on, the magnitude how far. b shifts the boundary, w sets its orientation — literally what fit learns.
In 2D the ratio of the coefficients gives the boundary's direction; the magnitude returns as confidence.
